'''Alan Osborne Trounson''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AO}} (born 16 February 1946) is an Australian [[embryologist]] who has made contributions to human in [[vitro fertilisation]] (IVF), [[Embryonic stem cell|embryonic stem cell research]], and [[regenerative medicine]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.australianoftheyear.org.au/honour-roll/?view=fullView&recipientID=934 |title=State Finalist Senior Australian of the Year 2013 |date=6 November 2012 |access-date=21 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130106122353/http://www.australianoftheyear.org.au/honour-roll/?view=fullView&recipientID=934|archive-date=6 January 2013}}</ref> He is an Emeritus Professor at [[Monash University]], a Distinguished Scientist at the [[Hudson Institute of Medical Research]], and the founder, CEO, and Executive Chair of Evinco Therapeutics. Trounson served as President of the [[California Institute for Regenerative Medicine]] (CIRM), California's $3 billion stem cell agency, from 2007 to 2014.<ref name="sn1">{{cite news |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/cirm-director-steps-down |title=CIRM Director Steps Down |work=Science Now |date=17 October 2013 |access-date=3 September 2016 |author=Kaiser, Jocelyn }}</ref><ref name="sn2">{{cite news |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/california-stem-cell-institute-picks-industry-veteran-president |title=California Stem Cell Institute Picks Industry Veteran as President |work=Science Now |date=30 April 2014 |access-date=3 September 2016 |author=Servick, Kelly }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Trounson grew up in [[New South Wales|rural New South Wales]], where he frequently visited school friends' farms and developed a love of animals, dreaming of becoming a farmer. He ultimately followed his father's advice, along with the attraction of multiple scholarships, and chose to study wool technology at the [[University of New South Wales]] rather than veterinary science.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-02-14 |title=Groundbreaking studies of sheep fertility helped develop human IVF and stem cells |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-02-14/landline-an-ivf-pioneers-journey-from-sheep-to-stem-cells/11964830 |access-date=2026-10-04 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref> He received a Master of Science from the [[University of New South Wales]] in 1971, researching the physiology and genetics of multiple births in sheep.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Top 10 Facts about Alan Truonson |url=https://www.discoverwalks.com/blog/australia/top-10-facts-about-alan-truonson/ |website=Discover walk}}</ref> He subsequently earned a PhD from the [[University of Sydney]] in 1974,<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Scientist to head top stem cell unit |url=https://www.telegram.com/story/news/local/north/2007/09/16/scientist-to-head-top-stem/52793664007/ |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=The Worcester Telegram & Gazette |language=en-US}}</ref> with a thesis titled "Studies on the Development of Fertilized Sheep Ova". From 1971 to 1976, Trounson was a Dalgety Fellow at the [[Australian Research Council]]'s Institute of Animal Physiology and Biochemistry at the [[University of Cambridge]]. There he focused on cattle embryo freezing, [[embryo transfer]], and embryo biology. He developed nonsurgical embryo collection and transfer techniques in cattle and pioneered embryo splitting and freezing in farm animals, techniques that later became the foundation of the global sheep and cattle reproductive technology industry.<ref name=eoas/>

== Career ==

=== Monash University and IVF research ===
In 1977, [[Carl Wood]], a pioneer of in vitro fertilization (IVF) and founder of [[Monash IVF]], invited Trounson to join his research team at [[Monash University]]. Although Trounson initially expected to work in IVF for only about a year, he became a major contributor to the development of human assisted reproductive technology.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-11 |title=The Monash researchers that pioneered IVF in Australia |url=https://www.monash.edu/medicine/news/latest/2022-articles/monash-researchers-pioneered-ivf-in-australia |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences |language=en}}</ref>

At Monash, Trounson and his colleagues contributed to several advances in [[In vitro fertilisation|IVF]], including controlled ovarian stimulation and the collection of multiple oocytes, embryo cryopreservation, egg and embryo donation, sperm microinjection, embryo biopsy for genetic and chromosomal analysis, in vitro maturation of oocytes, and vitrification of eggs and embryos. The Monash team was involved in 14 of the first 16 IVF births worldwide, and in 1980 Australia’s first IVF baby was born following the team's work.<ref>{{cite book |title=I.V.F. In Vitro Fertilisation |author1=Wood, Carl |author2=Riley, Robyn |publisher=New Edition |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-85572-212-8 }}</ref>

Trounson was appointed Reader in Obstetrics and Gynaecology at [[Monash University]] in 1984 and became Director of the Centre for Early Human Development in 1985. He was appointed to a Personal Chair in Obstetrics, Gynaecology and Paediatrics in 1991 and later held a Personal Chair in Stem Cell Sciences.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theage.com.au/national/stem-cell-pioneer-joins-science-exodus-20070916-ge5u3t.html |title=Stem cell pioneer joins science exodus |work=[[The Age]] |date=16 September 2007 |access-date=3 September 2016 |author= Weekes, Peter }}</ref>

=== Embryonic Stem Cell Research ===
In the mid-1990s, Trounson's research focus shifted from [[reproductive medicine]] to stem cells. He explained: "I became interested in studying hESCs as a way of exploring cell differentiation beyond the blastocyst stage." After Dr. James Thomson published his paper on the establishment of hESC lines in Science in 1998, Trounson submitted multiple grant applications to the Australian government, which "completely changed the whole direction of my research."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-02-09 |title=IVF pioneer, Alan Trounson, returns to the Institute |url=https://hudson.org.au/news/ivf-pioneer-alan-trounson-returns-to-the-institute/ |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=Hudson Institute of Medical Research |language=en-AU}}</ref>

In 2000, his team published a groundbreaking paper in ''Nature Biotechnology'' reporting the derivation of pluripotent embryonic stem cell lines from human blastocysts. The paper has been cited over 3,000 times. At the Monash Immunology and Stem Cell Laboratories (MISCL), his laboratory made several major advances, including the production and characterization of new embryonic stem cell lines, controlled differentiation of hESCs into pure nerve cells, and directed differentiation of mouse and human ESCs into respiratory, hepatic, and thymic progenitor lineages<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2000 |title=Erratum to "Embryonic stem cell lines from human blastocysts: somatic differentiation in vitro" |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt0500_559e |journal=Nature Biotechnology |language=en |volume=18 |issue=5 |pages=559 |doi=10.1038/75450 |issn=1087-0156}}</ref>

=== Australian Stem Cell Centre ===
Trounson was the founder and Executive Vice Chairman of the [[Australian Stem Cell Centre]] (ASCC), established in 2002 as the National Biotechnology Centre of Excellence. He left the ASCC in 2003 due to disagreements over the centre's commercialization focus.<ref name="autogenerated1">{{cite web|title=Cloning and Stem Cells |url=http://www.liebertpub.com/eboard.aspx?clo |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928002415/https://www.liebertpub.com/eboard.aspx?clo |archive-date=28 September 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|publisher=International Society for Stem Cell Research |title=ISSCR Officers |url=http://www.isscr.org/leadership/index.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070625132644/http://www.isscr.org/leadership/index.htm |archive-date=25 June 2007 }}</ref>

=== California Institute for Regenerative Medicine ===
In 2007, Trounson was appointed president of the [[California Institute for Regenerative Medicine]] (CIRM), which had been established by California voters through Proposition 71 to fund stem cell research.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2007-09-01 |title=California gets Australia's top stem-cell scientist |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/449271b |journal=Nature |language=en |publisher=Nature Publishing Group |volume=449 |issue=7160 |pages=271 |doi=10.1038/449271b |bibcode=2007Natur.449R.271. |issn=1476-4687}}</ref>

During his tenure, CIRM introduced or expanded several programs, including the Bridges and Creativity training programs, the Alpha Clinics initiative for translating experimental therapies into clinical care, the Stem Cell Genomics program, and an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPS cell) bank for research into complex diseases. Trounson served as CIRM president for nearly six years. In October 2013, he announced that he would step down from the position and return to Australia to spend more time with his family.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CIRM President Alan Trounson To Step Down – CIRM |url=https://www.cirm.ca.gov/about-cirm/newsroom/press-releases/10162013-cirm-president-alan-trounson-step-down/ |access-date=2026-10-04 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Biotechnology Entrepreneurship and Recent Work ===
Trounson has founded eight companies and one foundation, the latter providing low-cost IVF treatment in Africa. Cartherics Pty Ltd was founded by Trounson in 2016 to develop Chimeric Antigen Receptor Technology (CAR-T)/[[T-cell receptor|T Cell Receptor]] (TCR) therapies using induced [[Cell potency|Pluripotent Stem Cells]] (iPSCs) as an off-the-shelf approach for treating cancer.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chowdhry |first=Amit |date=2024-11-14 |title=Cartherics: Interview With CEO Prof. Alan Trounson About The Cell Therapy Company |url=https://pulse2.com/cartherics-profile-alan-trounson-interview/ |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=Pulse 2.0 |language=en}}</ref> The company is located at the Translation Research Facility Building, Monash Medical Centre, Clayton, Victoria. In 2025, Trounson handed over the CEO role to Dr. Ian Nisbet and became Deputy Chair of the Board.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cartherics appoints Dr Ian Nisbet as CEO as the company accelerates toward clinical trials |url=https://biotechdispatch.com.au/news/cartherics-appoints-dr-ian-nisbet-as-ceo-as-the-company-accelerates-toward-clinical-trials |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=biotechdispatch.com.au}}</ref> Evinco Therapeutics was spun out of Cartherics in December 2025 to develop advanced immune-based therapies for neurological disorders. Its initial research program involves [[extracellular vesicle]]s (EVs) derived from [[Natural killer cell|natural killer]] (NK) cells, delivered intranasally to target Alzheimer's disease and other neuroinflammatory conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Buntz |first=Brian |date=2026-05-22 |title=Traumatic brain injury and Alzheimer's disease, common neuroinflammatory pathologies and therapeutic potential |url=https://www.drugdiscoverytrends.com/traumatic-brain-injury-and-alzheimers-disease-common-neuroinflammatory-pathologies-and-therapeutic-potential/ |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=Drug Discovery and Development |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Controversy ==
In August 2002, [[Monash University]] asked Trounson to stop publicly discussing embryo and stem cell research due to sensitivities surrounding a A$43.5 million government grant approved three months earlier. His "offence" was showing a video of a paralysed rat that had regained the ability to walk with the help of embryonic stem cell research. Trounson told The Lancet that there was no intent to deceive, but that he had mistakenly overestimated the audience's knowledge. He explained: "These cells were embryonic germ cells—often defined as embryonic stem cells, they behave like embryonic stem cells, but they were taken from 6–8-week-old embryos, not 1-week-old embryos. In hindsight, I should have defined them strictly—which is sometimes a problem when discussing science with a lay audience.".<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theage.com.au/national/monash-uni-gags-trounson-as-mps-ban-cloning-20020830-gdujju.html |title=Monash Uni gags Trounson as MPs ban cloning |work=[[The Age]] |date=30 August 2002 |access-date=3 September 2016 |author1=Wroe, David |author2=Gray, Darren |author3=Douez, Sophie }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theage.com.au/national/uni-denies-gagging-trounson-20020830-gdujkg.html |title=Uni denies gagging Trounson |work=[[The Age]] |date=30 August 2002 |access-date=3 September 2016 |agency=[[Australian Associated Press]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.abc.net.au/am/stories/s661598.htm |title=Professor Trounson defends himself |author=Knight, Ben |work=AM |publisher=[[ABC Local Radio]] |location=Australia |date=29 August 2002 |access-date=3 September 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.abc.net.au/7.30/content/2002/s662263.htm |author=Kelly, Fran |author-link=Fran Kelly |title=Has Trounson affected the future of stem cell research? |work=[[7.30|The 7.30 Report]] |publisher=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation|ABC TV]] |location=Australia |date=29 August 2002 |access-date=3 September 2016 |format=Transcript |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515110657/http://www.abc.net.au/7.30/content/2002/s662263.htm |archive-date=15 May 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Research Areas ==
Trounson's research interests include [[cloning]], [[stem cells]], [[biotechnology]], cloning for the [[Agriculture|agricultural industry]], gene storage, and [[in vitro fertilisation]]. His clinical translation work includes reviews of stem cell therapies in clinical trials, noting that autologous and allogeneic transplants have shown few safety issues, that limbal stem cells have been registered in Europe for treating eye burns, and that [[mesenchymal stem cell]]s have been approved in Canada and New Zealand for pediatric graft-versus-host disease. His research output includes 168 articles, 46 abstracts, and 22 book chapters. Scopus data shows 504 documents, an h-index of 86, and 31,174 citations.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":5" />

== Documentary and media ==
In 2007, Magic Lantern Media Inc produced a documentary about Trounson titled ''Genetics, Stem Cells and Society'', featuring an interview with Trounson covering his beginnings in science, his pioneering IVF work, and his leadership role in embryonic stem cell research.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://cwc.wyldcatalog.org/CWCCREDOandFOD/1000141128 |title=Genetics, Stem Cells and Society |date=2007 |language=en |publisher=Magic Lantern Media Inc |access-date=2026-10-05 |via=cwc.wyldcatalog.org}}</ref>
